controlsTip.text: Tap for a hop, hold for a big jump — keep holding to flip, let go to land!
controlsTip.kid: Tap to hop! Hold for a big jump, and keep holding to flip!

relicTip.text: See that glow? Relics carry stories. Grab them!
relicTip.kid: Ooh, shiny! Grab the glowing relics!

winLines.text: We made it! Another realm's story is safe in the Codex.
Escaped! The old storytellers would be proud.

loseLines.text: Even heroes stumble. Myths are full of second tries.
loseLines.kid: Oops! Let's try again — heroes never give up!

facts.text: The Greeks pictured twelve Olympian gods living on Mount Olympus — a real peak, Greece's highest at about 2,918 m.
facts.kid: Greek gods lived on Mount Olympus — a real mountain you can climb today!

facts.text: Athens is named for Athena, goddess of wisdom. Her owl was stamped on Athenian silver coins.
facts.kid: The city of Athens is named after Athena, goddess of wisdom. Her bird was a wise owl!

facts.text: Greeks performed myths on stage at festivals for Dionysus — the roots of Western tragedy and comedy.
facts.kid: Greeks acted out myths in giant open-air theaters. That's where plays come from!

relic.name: Owl Tetradrachm
relic.text: Athens' silver 'owl' coin was so trusted that traders across the Mediterranean accepted it.
relic.kid: This silver owl coin was so trusted, people used it in many lands!

intro.text: Talos! The bronze giant who circled Crete three times a day — some call him an ancient idea of a robot. Run!
intro.kid: It's Talos, a giant made of bronze — like an ancient robot! Run, run!

facts.text: Egyptians believed the sun god Ra sailed a boat across the sky by day and through the underworld by night.
facts.kid: Egyptians thought the sun god Ra rode a boat across the sky every day!

facts.text: In the afterlife, your heart was weighed against the feather of Ma'at, goddess of truth. A light heart meant paradise.
facts.kid: In Egyptian stories, your heart was weighed against a feather. A kind, light heart was the goal!

facts.text: Hieroglyphs were a mystery for centuries until Jean-François Champollion cracked them in 1822 using the Rosetta Stone.
facts.kid: For ages nobody could read hieroglyphs — until a stone with three kinds of writing cracked the code!

relic.name: Scarab Amulet
relic.text: Scarab beetles roll balls of dung, so Egyptians imagined the god Khepri rolling the sun across the sky.
relic.kid: Scarab beetles roll balls of dung — Egyptians imagined a beetle god rolling the sun!

intro.text: Apep, serpent of chaos! Each night it attacked Ra's sun-boat — and each dawn, it lost. Let's make sure it loses again!
intro.kid: Apep, the giant chaos snake, tries to stop the sun every night. Zoom past it!

facts.text: Norse myth places nine worlds among the branches and roots of Yggdrasil, a giant ash tree at the center of everything.
facts.kid: Vikings told of a giant tree called Yggdrasil holding up nine whole worlds!

facts.text: You say Norse gods every week: Wednesday is Woden's (Odin's) day, and Thursday is Thor's day.
facts.kid: Thursday means 'Thor's day' — named after the thunder god with the hammer!

facts.text: Odin's ravens Huginn and Muninn — 'Thought' and 'Memory' — flew over the world each day and brought him news.
facts.kid: Odin had two raven friends who flew around the world and told him the news every day!

relic.name: Rune Stone
relic.text: Runes were the Norse alphabet. The Viking Age 'Younger Futhark' used just 16 letters.
relic.kid: Vikings wrote with runes — straight-line letters that are easy to carve in wood and stone!

intro.text: Fenrir! The gods bound this giant wolf with a ribbon made of impossible things — like the sound of a cat's footsteps. It's loose!
intro.kid: Fenrir the giant wolf got loose! Quick, outrun him!

facts.text: When sun goddess Amaterasu hid in a cave, the world went dark. The gods lured her out with laughter, music and a mirror.
facts.kid: The sun goddess once hid in a cave and the world went dark! A party and a mirror brought her out.

facts.text: In Shinto, kami — spirits — can dwell in mountains, trees and waterfalls. Torii gates mark the way into sacred space.
facts.kid: Japanese stories say spirits called kami live in trees and mountains. Red gates show sacred places!

facts.text: The Kojiki, finished in 712 CE, is Japan's oldest surviving book. It records myths of the islands' creation.
facts.kid: Japan's oldest book, the Kojiki, is over 1,300 years old and full of myths!

relic.name: Kusanagi Sword
relic.text: Legend says the storm god Susanoo found the sword Kusanagi inside a tail of the serpent Orochi.
relic.kid: A magic sword was found inside the tail of a giant snake — and became a royal treasure!

intro.text: Yamata no Orochi — eight heads, eight tails! Susanoo beat it by tricking it into drinking strong sake.
intro.kid: An eight-headed dragon! Long ago a hero tricked it into a big sleepy nap. Let's be clever too!

facts.text: Legend says the Mexica founded Tenochtitlan where they saw an eagle on a cactus. That scene is on Mexico's flag today.
facts.kid: The Aztecs built their city where they saw an eagle on a cactus — look at Mexico's flag!

facts.text: Tenochtitlan stood on an island in Lake Texcoco, linked by causeways and fed by floating gardens called chinampas.
facts.kid: The Aztec capital sat on a lake, with floating gardens for growing food!

facts.text: Chocolate, tomato and avocado come from Nahuatl, the Aztec language — still spoken by over a million people.
facts.kid: The words chocolate, tomato and avocado come from the Aztec language!

relic.name: Sun Stone
relic.text: The 24-ton Aztec Sun Stone was rediscovered in 1790 during repairs to Mexico City's main square.
relic.kid: A giant carved stone as heavy as four elephants was found under Mexico City!

intro.text: Cipactli, the giant earth crocodile! In Aztec myth, the gods shaped the world from its body.
intro.kid: A huge crocodile monster! Aztec stories say the land was made from its body. Hop to it!

facts.text: Halloween grew partly from Samhain, a Gaelic festival when the boundary between our world and the Otherworld grew thin.
facts.kid: Halloween comes partly from an old Irish festival when spirits were said to wander close by!

facts.text: Newgrange, a passage tomb older than the Great Pyramid, lights up inside at sunrise on the winter solstice.
facts.kid: An Irish tomb over 5,000 years old lights up inside on the shortest day of the year!

facts.text: Ogham, an early Irish alphabet, was carved as notches along the edges of standing stones.
facts.kid: Early Irish people wrote by cutting little lines along the edges of stones!

relic.name: Spear of Lugh
relic.text: Lugh, master of every craft, gave his name to Lughnasadh, a harvest festival still marked in Ireland.
relic.kid: Lugh was good at every job! An Irish summer festival is still named after him.

intro.text: Balor of the Evil Eye — one look from his giant eye could destroy armies. Keep moving and don't look back!
intro.kid: Balor has one giant grumpy eye. Don't let him spot you — go go go!

realms.name: Riverlands of the Vedas

facts.text: The Rigveda, composed over 3,000 years ago, is among the oldest religious texts still recited today.
facts.kid: Some Hindu hymns are over 3,000 years old — and people still sing them today!

facts.text: The Mahabharata has roughly 100,000 verses, making it one of the longest poems ever composed.
facts.kid: The Mahabharata is one of the longest poems in the world — about 100,000 verses!

facts.text: For many Hindus, Diwali's lamps celebrate Rama's return home to Ayodhya after defeating the demon king Ravana.
facts.kid: Diwali is a festival of lights! Lamps welcome the hero Rama home after a big adventure.

relic.name: Conch Shell
relic.text: The shankha, a conch-shell trumpet, is blown in Hindu temples. Vishnu is often shown holding one.
relic.kid: This shell is a trumpet! It's blown in temples, and the god Vishnu holds one too.

intro.text: Vritra, the drought serpent of the Rigveda, coiled around the rivers to stop them flowing. Set the waters free!
intro.kid: A giant snake is blocking the rivers! Let's race past it and set the water free!

realms.review: Living religion: have a Hindu cultural consultant review tone and imagery.

facts.text: The Epic of Gilgamesh, first written in Mesopotamia about 4,000 years ago, is one of the oldest stories ever recorded.
facts.kid: Gilgamesh is one of the oldest written stories in the world — about 4,000 years old!

facts.text: Sumerians developed one of the first writing systems, cuneiform — wedge-shaped marks pressed into wet clay.
facts.kid: Sumerians wrote by pressing wedge shapes into clay. It's one of the first kinds of writing!

facts.text: Our 60-minute hour and 360-degree circle trace back to Mesopotamia's base-60 number system.
facts.kid: Why are there 60 minutes in an hour? Thank the ancient people of Mesopotamia!

relic.name: Clay Tablet
relic.text: Hundreds of thousands of cuneiform tablets survive — from epic poems to letters, laws and shopping receipts.
relic.kid: Thousands of clay tablets survive — stories, letters, even shopping lists!

intro.text: Humbaba, guardian of the Cedar Forest — his roar is a flood, his breath is fire. Gilgamesh faced him; now it's your turn!
intro.kid: Humbaba guards the cedar forest and roars like a flood! Let's be brave like Gilgamesh!

realms.name: Crown of Ilé-Ifẹ̀

facts.text: In Yoruba tradition, Ọbàtálá climbed down a chain from the sky with soil in a snail shell. A hen spread it into land at Ilé-Ifẹ̀.
facts.kid: A Yoruba story says the first land was made from soil in a snail shell, spread out by a hen!

facts.text: Ṣàngó, the Òrìṣà of thunder and lightning, is remembered as a powerful king of the old Ọ̀yọ́ empire.
facts.kid: Ṣàngó is the Yoruba spirit of thunder — said to have once been a mighty king!

facts.text: Yoruba beliefs crossed the Atlantic and live on today in Brazil's Candomblé and Cuba's Santería.
facts.kid: Yoruba traditions traveled across the ocean and are still celebrated in Brazil and Cuba!

relic.name: Ifá Tray
relic.text: Ifá, the Yoruba system of divination and wisdom verses, is recognized by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage.
relic.kid: Ifá is a Yoruba treasure of wise sayings — protected as world heritage!

intro.text: In one telling, Olókun, ruler of the deep, sent a great flood over the land. Outrun the rising tide!
intro.kid: The sea is rising up in a giant wave! Run for high ground!

realms.review: Living tradition: Òrìṣà must never be framed as enemies. Have a Yoruba practitioner review.

realms.name: Fish of Māui

facts.text: Māui fished up the North Island with a magic hook. Its Māori name, Te Ika-a-Māui, means 'the fish of Māui.'
facts.kid: The hero Māui fished up a whole island! It's still called 'the fish of Māui.'

facts.text: Ranginui (Sky Father) and Papatūānuku (Earth Mother) held each other tight until their son Tāne pushed them apart to let in light.
facts.kid: Sky Father and Earth Mother hugged so tight it was dark — until their son pushed them apart for light!

facts.text: Māui also snared the sun with ropes to slow it down, giving people longer days.
facts.kid: Māui lassoed the sun to slow it down, so days would be longer!

relic.name: Pounamu
relic.text: Pounamu, New Zealand greenstone, is treasured as taonga and passed down through generations.
relic.kid: This greenstone is a family treasure, handed down from grandparents to grandkids!

intro.text: A taniwha! These powerful beings guard rivers and caves. This one is testing you — show it your speed!
intro.kid: A river guardian called a taniwha wants to see how fast you are. Show it!

realms.review: Living culture: taniwha are often protectors. Keep framing as a test, and consult Māori advisors.

facts.text: In one Chinese creation story, the giant Pangu pushed sky and earth apart. When he died, his body became mountains, rivers and stars.
facts.kid: A giant named Pangu pushed the sky up high. His body became mountains and rivers!

facts.text: Chinese dragons aren't villains — they bring rain and good fortune, and were symbols of the emperor.
facts.kid: In China, dragons are lucky! They bring rain for the crops.

facts.text: Chang'e, goddess of the Moon, gave her name to China's lunar probes — Chang'e 4 landed on the Moon's far side in 2019.
facts.kid: China's Moon robots are named after Chang'e, the Moon goddess!

relic.name: Red Envelope
relic.text: Red envelopes of money are given at Lunar New Year — red was said to scare away the beast Nian.
relic.kid: At Lunar New Year, kids get red envelopes. Red scares away the monster Nian!

intro.text: Nian! This beast raided villages each new year until people learned it feared red, firecrackers and loud noise.
intro.kid: Nian is a beast that's scared of the color red and loud bangs! Zoom away!

realms.name: Popol Vuh Canopy

facts.text: The Popol Vuh, the K'iche' Maya book of creation, says the gods finally made people out of maize dough.
facts.kid: A Maya story says the first people were made from corn!

facts.text: The Maya used a symbol for zero centuries before the idea reached Europe.
facts.kid: The Maya used the number zero long, long before Europe did!

facts.text: Millions of Maya people live today, speaking around 30 Mayan languages.
facts.kid: The Maya are still here! Millions of Maya people live in Central America today.

relic.name: Cacao Beans
relic.text: Cacao beans were so valuable in Mesoamerica that they were used as money.
relic.kid: Chocolate beans used to be money! Imagine paying with chocolate!

intro.text: Seven Macaw, the boastful bird who claimed to be the sun! In the Popol Vuh, the Hero Twins brought him down.
intro.kid: A show-off macaw says he's the sun! The Hero Twins outsmarted him — let's do it too!

realms.review: Living descendants: consult Maya cultural advisors on imagery.

facts.text: Baba Yaga, the forest witch of Slavic tales, lives in a hut that walks on giant chicken legs.
facts.kid: Baba Yaga's house walks around on giant chicken legs! Would you knock on that door?

facts.text: Perun, the Slavic god of thunder, was linked with mighty oak trees and battled the serpent-god Veles.
facts.kid: Perun, the thunder god, loved big oak trees and threw lightning bolts!

facts.text: Many families honored a domovoi, a house spirit, by leaving it bread and milk.
facts.kid: Slavic homes had a little house spirit called a domovoi. Families left it snacks!

relic.name: Firebird Feather
relic.text: In the tales, one Firebird feather glows bright enough to light a room. The story inspired Stravinsky's 1910 ballet.
relic.kid: In the stories, one Firebird feather glows like a lamp!

intro.text: Koschei the Deathless! He hid his death in a needle, in an egg, in a duck, in a hare, in an iron chest. Keep running!
intro.kid: Koschei hid his weakness inside an egg inside a duck inside a hare! Silly — and spooky. Run!

realms.name: Valley of the Storm Serpent

facts.text: In Zulu tradition, uNkulunkulu, the first ancestor, emerged from a bed of reeds and brought people and animals with him.
facts.kid: A Zulu story says the first person came out of a patch of reeds!

facts.text: Zulu beadwork can carry messages — colors and patterns in an ucu necklace could say 'I love you.'
facts.kid: Zulu beads can be secret messages! Colors and patterns can even say 'I love you.'

facts.text: Under King Shaka in the early 1800s, the Zulu grew from a small clan into a powerful kingdom.
facts.kid: King Shaka turned a small Zulu clan into a huge kingdom about 200 years ago!

relic.name: Ucu Beads
relic.text: In Zulu beadwork each color carries meanings — white often stands for love and purity.
relic.kid: In Zulu beadwork, white beads often mean love!

intro.text: Inkanyamba, the giant storm serpent! Zulu and Xhosa stories blame it for the whirling summer tornadoes.
intro.kid: A giant serpent made of storm winds! Outrun the whirlwind!

realms.review: Living culture: consult Zulu cultural advisors.

realms.name: Sedna's Ice Sea

facts.text: Sedna, the sea woman, is mother of seals, whales and walruses. Hunters showed respect so she would share them.
facts.kid: Sedna lives under the sea and takes care of the seals and whales!

facts.text: In some Inuit stories, the northern lights are spirits playing a ball game across the sky.
facts.kid: Some Inuit stories say the northern lights are spirits playing ball in the sky!

facts.text: An inuksuk, a stone figure, can mark a route, a good fishing spot or a place to remember. One is on Nunavut's flag.
facts.kid: Inuksuks are stone figures that show travelers the way. One is on a flag!

relic.name: Snow Goggles
relic.text: Inuit snow goggles, carved from bone, antler or wood with thin slits, protected eyes from snow blindness.
relic.kid: Inuit invented snow goggles with tiny slits to protect eyes from bright snow!

intro.text: Qalupalik! Parents told of this sea creature so children would stay away from thin ice and the water's edge.
intro.kid: Qalupalik is a story that keeps kids safe from thin ice! Stay on solid ground and run!

realms.review: Living culture: stories vary by community. Consult Inuit advisors (e.g. via Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami).

facts.text: Ferdowsi spent about 30 years writing the Shahnameh, an epic of some 50,000 couplets that helped preserve the Persian language.
facts.kid: A poet spent 30 years writing one giant book of Persian legends — the Shahnameh!

facts.text: The Simurgh, a giant wise bird, raised the hero Zal in her nest on Mount Alborz.
facts.kid: A giant kind bird called the Simurgh raised a baby hero in her nest!

facts.text: Nowruz, the Persian New Year, begins at the spring equinox and is celebrated by an estimated 300 million people.
facts.kid: Nowruz is a New Year party on the first day of spring, celebrated by millions!

relic.name: Simurgh Feather
relic.text: In the Shahnameh, the Simurgh gave Zal feathers to burn whenever he needed her help.
relic.kid: Burn a Simurgh feather, and the giant bird comes to help!

intro.text: The White Div! The hero Rostam fought this demon in a cave during his Seven Labors. Be as swift as Rostam's horse Rakhsh!
intro.kid: A big white monster! The hero Rostam beat it with help from his brave horse. Gallop!

realms.name: Fire Islands

facts.text: Polynesian navigators reached Hawaiʻi without instruments, reading stars, swells and birds. The canoe Hōkūleʻa proved it again in 1976.
facts.kid: Long ago, sailors found Hawaiʻi using only the stars, waves and birds — no maps!

facts.text: Māui is said to have snared the sun from the summit of Haleakalā — the 'House of the Sun' — to make days longer.
facts.kid: Māui caught the sun from a giant volcano called the 'House of the Sun'!

facts.text: Hula is more than dance: its chants and movements carry history, genealogy and stories of the land.
facts.kid: Hula dances tell stories! Every move means something.

relic.name: Star Compass
relic.text: Navigators memorized where dozens of stars rise and set on the horizon — a 'star compass' held in the mind.
relic.kid: Hawaiian navigators kept a map of the stars in their heads!

intro.text: The volcano wakes! Hawaiians honor it as the home of Pele, goddess of fire. Respect her power — and run!
intro.kid: Hot lava is flowing! Volcanoes make new land in Hawaiʻi. Run ahead!

realms.review: Living culture: Pele is a revered deity — never depict her as an enemy. Consult Native Hawaiian advisors.

realms.name: Sky Roads of the Andes

facts.text: The Inca had no written alphabet, but they kept numbers and records on quipu — knotted strings.
facts.kid: The Inca kept records with knots on strings instead of writing!

facts.text: Inti Raymi, the Inca Festival of the Sun, is still celebrated in Cusco every June 24th.
facts.kid: The Inca Sun Festival is still celebrated every June in Peru!

facts.text: The Inca road network, the Qhapaq Ñan, stretched about 30,000 km across mountains, deserts and jungle.
facts.kid: The Inca built roads so long they could stretch most of the way around the Earth!

relic.name: Quipu
relic.text: Trained record-keepers called quipucamayocs read a quipu by the color, position and type of its knots.
relic.kid: Each knot's color and position meant something — like a secret code!

intro.text: Amaru, the great serpent of the Andes, linked the underworld and the sky. Here it comes!
intro.kid: Amaru is a giant mountain serpent! Climb fast!

realms.review: Quechua and Aymara peoples are living descendants: consult Andean cultural advisors.

facts.text: Elias Lönnrot traveled thousands of kilometers collecting folk songs, publishing them as the Kalevala in 1835.
facts.kid: A doctor traveled across Finland collecting old songs and turned them into one epic book!

facts.text: Väinämöinen, the wise old singer, built a kantele harp from the jawbone of a giant pike.
facts.kid: The wise hero Väinämöinen made a harp out of a giant fish's jawbone!

facts.text: J.R.R. Tolkien loved the Kalevala, and Finnish helped inspire his Elvish language, Quenya.
facts.kid: The author of The Hobbit loved these stories so much, Finnish inspired his Elf language!

relic.name: Sampo Shard
relic.text: The Sampo, forged by the smith Ilmarinen, was a magic mill that ground out grain, salt and gold.
relic.kid: The Sampo was a magic mill that made food, salt and gold forever!

intro.text: Louhi, Mistress of the North, turned into a giant eagle to chase the heroes who took the Sampo! Fly!
intro.kid: Louhi turned into a giant eagle! Run, run!

realms.name: Anansi's Web Forest

facts.text: Anansi the spider bought all the world's stories from the sky god Nyame — so Akan folktales are called Anansesem, 'spider stories.'
facts.kid: Anansi the clever spider bought all the stories in the world from the sky god!

facts.text: The Golden Stool is said to have come down from the sky around 1701. It holds the soul of the Asante nation — no one sits on it.
facts.kid: The Asante have a Golden Stool from the sky — so special that nobody ever sits on it!

facts.text: Anansi stories crossed the Atlantic, becoming 'Aunt Nancy' tales in the Americas.
facts.kid: Anansi stories sailed across the ocean and are told in the Caribbean too!

relic.name: Sankofa Stamp
relic.text: Sankofa, an Adinkra symbol, means 'go back and get it' — learn from the past to build the future.
relic.kid: The Sankofa bird looks backward. It means: learn from the past!

intro.text: Sasabonsam! This forest creature hangs from tall trees and swoops on travelers. Don't linger under the branches!
intro.kid: A spooky tree creature! Keep moving through the forest!

realms.review: Living culture: consult Akan cultural advisors.

facts.text: Many Mongols honored Tengri, the Eternal Blue Sky. Blue silk scarves called khadag are still offered as a sign of respect.
facts.kid: Mongolian stories honor the Eternal Blue Sky. People give blue scarves as gifts of respect!

facts.text: Travelers walk around an ovoo, a sacred stone cairn, three times clockwise and add a stone for a safe journey.
facts.kid: When you pass a stone pile called an ovoo, walk around it three times and add a stone for luck!

facts.text: Naadam, the 'Three Games of Men,' still celebrates wrestling, horse racing and archery each summer.
facts.kid: At the Naadam festival, people race horses, wrestle and shoot arrows!

relic.name: Khadag Scarf
relic.text: A khadag is offered with both hands as a sign of respect at greetings and ceremonies.
relic.kid: Give a blue scarf with both hands — it's a big hello of respect!

intro.text: A mangus! These many-headed ogres battle heroes like King Geser in Mongolian epics. Ride like the wind!
intro.kid: A many-headed ogre! The hero Geser beat lots of them. Ride like the wind!

facts.text: Hittite is the oldest written Indo-European language — a distant relative of English, Hindi and Persian.
facts.kid: Hittite is the oldest written language in the family that includes English!

facts.text: After the Battle of Kadesh, the Hittites and Egypt signed one of the earliest known peace treaties, around 1259 BCE.
facts.kid: The Hittites and Egypt made one of the world's first peace treaties, over 3,000 years ago!

facts.text: The Hittites called their realm 'the land of a thousand gods,' adopting gods from the peoples they met.
facts.kid: The Hittites had so many gods, they called their home 'the land of a thousand gods'!

relic.name: Treaty Tablet
relic.text: A replica of the Hittite–Egyptian peace treaty tablet hangs at the United Nations headquarters in New York.
relic.kid: A copy of this ancient peace deal hangs at the United Nations today!

intro.text: Illuyanka, the dragon-serpent! In one version, it feasted until it was too fat to escape — then the storm god struck.
intro.kid: Illuyanka is a dragon who ate so much at a party it got stuck! Zoom past!

realms.name: Birdman Isle

facts.text: Nearly 1,000 moai were carved, most from the volcanic rock of the Rano Raraku quarry.
facts.kid: People on Rapa Nui carved almost 1,000 giant stone statues called moai!

facts.text: Most moai face inland, watching over villages — they represent honored ancestors.
facts.kid: Most moai face away from the sea, watching over their families like guardians!

facts.text: Rongorongo, a script carved on wooden tablets, has never been deciphered.
facts.kid: Rapa Nui has a mystery writing called rongorongo that no one can read yet!

relic.name: Manutara Egg
relic.text: In the Birdman contest, racers swam to an islet to bring back the season's first sooty tern egg.
relic.kid: In the Birdman race, swimmers raced to find the first bird egg of spring!

intro.text: The Tangata Manu race! Champions climbed cliffs and swam to Motu Nui for the first tern egg. Race the rival!
intro.kid: It's the Birdman race! Beat the champion to the egg!

realms.review: Living culture: consult Rapa Nui advisors on moai imagery.

realms.name: Hurricane Coast

facts.text: 'Hurricane' comes from the Taíno storm force Juracán. 'Hammock,' 'canoe' and 'barbecue' are Taíno words too.
facts.kid: The words hurricane, hammock and canoe all come from the Taíno people!

facts.text: Yúcahu was the Taíno spirit of cassava and the sea. Many cemí carvings have three points like a mountain.
facts.kid: Taíno people carved three-pointed stones called cemís for good harvests!

facts.text: Studies find many Puerto Ricans today carry Taíno ancestry — the culture never fully disappeared.
facts.kid: Taíno family lines continue in the Caribbean today!

relic.name: Cemí Stone
relic.text: Cemís — carved in stone, wood or bone — held spirit power and were kept in homes and ceremonial places.
relic.kid: A cemí is a carved spirit stone for good luck!

intro.text: Juracán! The Taíno knew these spinning storms well — and gave the world the word 'hurricane.' Outrun the eye!
intro.kid: A huge spinning storm — a hurricane! Outrun it!

realms.review: Taíno revival communities exist today: consult them.

facts.text: The Etruscans ruled much of Italy before Rome rose — and early Rome itself had Etruscan kings.
facts.kid: Before Rome was famous, the Etruscans ruled Italy — they even had kings in Rome!

facts.text: Etruscan priests called haruspices read the will of the gods in the livers of sacrificed sheep.
facts.kid: Etruscan priests searched for messages from the gods in very unusual places!

facts.text: We can sound out Etruscan writing, but much of the language's meaning is still a mystery.
facts.kid: We can read Etruscan letters out loud — but we still don't know what most words mean!

relic.name: Liver of Piacenza
relic.text: The Bronze Liver of Piacenza is a model liver divided into regions, each labeled with a god's name.
relic.kid: This bronze map has gods' names written all over it — a guide for priests!

intro.text: The Chimera — lion, goat and serpent in one! Etruscan artists cast a famous bronze of it around 400 BCE.
intro.kid: A lion with a goat head on its back and a snake for a tail! Run!

realms.name: Cliffs of Bandiagara

facts.text: The Dogon built villages along the Bandiagara Escarpment, a cliff about 150 km long — now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
facts.kid: The Dogon live along giant cliffs — their villages are a world treasure!

facts.text: Before the Dogon, the Tellem people lived in small dwellings high in the cliffs — some still hold their granaries.
facts.kid: Long before, people called the Tellem built tiny homes high up in the cliffs!

facts.text: Dama masked dances honor the dead and help guide their spirits from the village to the afterlife.
facts.kid: Dogon dancers wear tall masks to say goodbye to loved ones and guide their spirits.

relic.name: Kanaga Mask
relic.text: The Kanaga mask, topped by a double-barred cross shape, is one of the best-known Dogon masks.
relic.kid: This mask has a tall shape like a bird or a person with arms out!

intro.text: The Harmattan! This dry, dusty wind blows off the Sahara every winter. Outrun the wall of dust!
intro.kid: A giant dust storm is blowing from the desert! Run ahead of the wind!

realms.review: Living culture with sacred masks: consult Dogon advisors before depicting masks.

realms.name: Kamuy Forest
realms.era: Recognized as Indigenous by Japan in 2019

facts.text: Ainu tradition holds that kamuy — gods — visit the human world wearing animal forms, like bears and owls.
facts.kid: Ainu stories say gods visit our world dressed up as animals, like bears!

facts.text: Kotan-kor-kamuy, the Blakiston's fish owl, was honored as the god who protects the village.
facts.kid: A giant owl was the protector of Ainu villages!

facts.text: Yukar are long epic songs passed down by memory. Japan officially recognized the Ainu as an Indigenous people in 2019.
facts.kid: Ainu stories were sung from memory for hundreds of years!

relic.name: Ikupasuy
relic.text: An ikupasuy is a carved prayer stick used to offer drops of drink and words to the kamuy.
relic.kid: This carved stick carries prayers to the gods!

intro.text: A blizzard sweeps down from the north! In Ainu stories, even the wind has a spirit — keep moving!
intro.kid: A big snowstorm is coming! Stay warm by moving fast!

realms.review: Living culture: consult Ainu advisors (e.g. Upopoy National Ainu Museum).

realms.name: Seven Monsters Jungle
realms.era: Guaraní is an official language of Paraguay

facts.text: Guaraní is an official language of Paraguay alongside Spanish, and most Paraguayans speak it.
facts.kid: In Paraguay, most people speak Guaraní — an Indigenous language!

facts.text: 'Jaguar' comes from the Tupi-Guaraní word yaguara. 'Piranha' and 'toucan' have Tupi-Guaraní roots too.
facts.kid: The words jaguar and toucan come from the Tupi-Guaraní languages!

facts.text: A Guaraní legend says the yerba mate plant was a gift from the moon goddess Yasí to an old man who saved her.
facts.kid: A legend says the Moon gave people the mate plant to say thank you!

relic.name: Mate Gourd
relic.text: Mate, a tea of yerba leaves, is shared from one gourd passed around a circle of friends.
relic.kid: Mate tea is shared from one cup passed around friends!

intro.text: Teju Jagua! First of the seven legendary monsters — a giant lizard with seven dog-like heads. Hop!
intro.kid: A giant lizard with seven heads! Hop hop hop!

facts.text: When the moon vanished in an eclipse, people said the sea serpent Bakunawa had swallowed it — and banged pots to make it spit it out.
facts.kid: When the moon vanished, people banged pots so the sea dragon Bakunawa would spit it out!

facts.text: Legend says there were once seven moons, and Bakunawa swallowed six; the moon we see is the last one.
facts.kid: A legend says there were once seven moons, and Bakunawa ate six of them!

facts.text: Bohol's Chocolate Hills — over 1,200 grassy mounds — appear in legends as boulders hurled by battling giants.
facts.kid: Over 1,200 hills that look like chocolate drops! Legends say giants threw them in a fight.

relic.name: Baybayin Script
relic.text: Baybayin, a pre-colonial Philippine script, is being revived today on signs, art and logos.
relic.kid: Filipinos had their own old alphabet, Baybayin — and people are learning it again!

intro.text: Bakunawa rises from the sea to swallow the moon! Make some noise — and get moving!
intro.kid: Bakunawa wants to eat the moon! Let's go save it!

realms.name: Painted Rocks of the Kalahari
realms.era: Rock art from c. 27,000 years ago

facts.text: Painted stones found in Namibia's Apollo 11 Cave are around 27,000 years old — some of Africa's oldest known art.
facts.kid: Painted stones found in Namibia are about 27,000 years old — some of the oldest art in Africa!

facts.text: In /Xam San stories, /Kaggen the Mantis threw his shoe into the sky, and it became the moon.
facts.kid: A trickster mantis threw his shoe into the sky — and it became the moon!

facts.text: San peoples are among the oldest continuous cultures on Earth, and their trance dances are still used for healing.
facts.kid: The San are one of the oldest cultures on Earth, and still dance to heal people!

relic.name: Ostrich Eggshell Beads
relic.text: Beads cut from ostrich eggshell have been made in Africa for over 40,000 years — San artisans still make them.
relic.kid: People have made beads from ostrich eggs for over 40,000 years!

intro.text: The All-Devourer! In a /Xam story it swallowed everything in its path — even trees. Don't be next!
intro.kid: The All-Devourer eats everything — even trees! Don't let it catch you!

realms.review: Living culture: consult San representatives (e.g. South African San Council).
